data.title: Tracking U.S., state and county gas prices, in maps and charts
data.description: The war in Iran has led to higher prices at the gas pump. Gas prices in the United States, up by more than 40% since the U.S. and Israel launched the war, have soared as the global oil supply constricts. Now at a national average of more than $4 per gallon, according to data from motor club AAA, this price increase is straining already-stretched budgets in households across the country. NBC News is tracking gas prices and how they change at the national, state and county levels, and will be updating this article daily with the latest data. Average gas prices have increased more than a dollar since the U.S. and Israel first attacked Iran. In four states — California, Hawaii, Nevada and Washington — average gas prices are at least $5 per gallon. Georgia, North Carolina and Texas are paying the least, according to AAA data. According to a Brown University analysis, the increase in gas prices since the start of the war has cost Americans more than $70 billion. Fuel costs aren’t limited to gas. Jet fuel prices have been surging as well, leading airlines to increase airfares. Oil prices have spiked, then see-sawed, were approaching pre-war levels, and are now surging again as turmoil in the Middle East continues. Since mid-May, the average national gas price has declined by around 20 cents. The average price is still up more than a dollar per gallon since the start of the war.

data.title: Polymarket trading halted after vendor compromise; impacted users will be ‘made whole’
data.description: Predictions markets platform Polymarket was forced to halt trading on its international platform Thursday for nearly an hour because of what it said was a third-party compromise. There were also unconfirmed reports from users on Polymarket’s Discord channel who said their wallets had been drained. While Polymarket did not confirm that users had lost money, it said “anyone who has been impacted will be made whole.” “We’ll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders,” the company said in a subsequent post on X. Crypto news website The Block reported some $2.65 million in cryptocurrencies had been siphoned from the platform, citing data from blockchain analysis group Arkham. In a statement posted on its X account, Polymarket said it had identified and fixed an issue affecting its international platform, Polymarket.com. “One of our 3rd party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement,” Polymarket said. “Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily halted trading & are working to bring the platform back online,” it added. Trading began again at 3 p.m. ET after nearly an hour offline. Polymarket’s U.S.-based platform did not appear to be affected by the breach. Compromises of third party vendors are a very common way malicious actors gain access to large platforms and websites. But Polymarket’s acknowledgement that hackers succeeded in stealing money from its users makes this a significant breach. Polymarket was valued at $21 billion in September after a group of investors led by Donald Trump Jr. invested $1 billion into the platform. The platform, along with rival Kalshi, have become to subject of an intense, multi-million-dollar battle between U.S. states and the Trump administration over who gets to regulate the prediction-market betting that occurs on the sites. The platforms also continue to fight off insider-trading threats. Earlier Thursday, Bloomberg News reported Polymarket was investigating reports of suspicious bets made amid Israel’s closely watched elections. It is also investigating “dozens” related to the U.S. midterms, according to the company’s head of global intelligence and investigations, Shana Bautista. Earlier this month, Kalshi said it was looking into suspicious bets involving Trump’s choice of press secretary.

data.title: DoorDash to acquire Instacart for $17 billion, creating delivery giant
data.description: Delivery giant DoorDash is buying to-your-door grocery service Instacart for $17 billion, the company announced Thursday. The deal means users will be able to order groceries and items from other retailers via DoorDash and its delivery network. The companies said Instacart customers can now shop at more than 50,000 additional stores on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today. DashPass and Instacart+ members will now also pay one membership fee instead of two. DoorDash is expected to keep the Instacart brand and its technology. Until the transaction closes, DoorDash and Instacart will continue to operate as separate and independent companies. “Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more,” said Chris Rogers, CEO of Instacart. The deal represents the latest chapter of consolidation in the delivery industry. Last year, DoorDash bought UK-based Deliveroo, while Uber now owns Postmates ​and Delivery Hero. DoorDash has emerged as the most successful stand-alone online delivery platform in America, commanding some two-thirds of all food-delivery volumes as of 2024, according to Bloomberg data. But over the past year, the company has seen its share price decline by approximately a third, largely due to rising costs. Instacart, meanwhile, reached the pinnacle of its success during the Covid-19 pandemic, when lockdowns sent millions of consumers to their phones to order up groceries. But the company’s stock has gone nowhere over the past two years, as Instacart struggled to find new paths to growth while facing increasing competition from Amazon and Walmart’s grocery-delivery offerings. While a merger would create cost-savings by allowing the combined company to reduce its corporate workforce and split some expenses, it’s not clear how much more money there remains that can be squeezed out of delivery customers. U.S. at-home eaters have begun to complain about the price of food delivery — and the pinch has only worsened this year amid soaring fuel costs, which have led to new fees and surcharges. A recent debate about the cost of having a burrito delivered went viral, as social media users argued over whether $20 was a reasonable price to pay to have the Tex-Mex treat delivered. Platforms like DoorDash and Instacart have also faced legal scrutiny over how they treat workers who deliver for their respective platforms. Last month, DoorDash settled with New York City regulators for $131.5 million to resolve charges it deprived workers of millions of dollars in tips. “Simply put, we screwed up,” the San ‌Francisco-based ⁠company said in a statement. “Our mistakes meant some Dashers were underpaid or paid late. While these mistakes weren’t intentional, that doesn’t make them okay.” The proposed transaction was first reported by tech website The Information and The Wall Street Journal.

data.title: Wendy’s, struggling with beef prices and growing competition, gets a buyout offer
data.description: Wendy’s shares jumped more than 14% Wednesday after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores. Peltz’s Trian Fund Management and several partners are offering Wendy’s $7.35 per share in cash, or a premium of nearly 19% over the stock’s closing price on Tuesday, in a deal that would take the company private. The offer values Wendy’s at $1.4 billion. Wendy’s, which is based in Dublin, Ohio, confirmed receipt of the unsolicited proposal in a statement Wednesday and said its board has formed an independent committee to evaluate it. At the end of last year, Wendy’s had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries. Wendy’s, founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald’s and Burger King, Wendy’s launched salad bars and ran its iconic “Where’s the beef?” ad campaign. But as the fast-food market grew even more competitive and rival burger-focused chains like In-N-Out and Five Guys expanded, Wendy’s fell behind. Wendy’s share of U.S. burger chain sales fell from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% last year, according to Technomic, a market research company. In recent years, inflation has also hurt Wendy’s and other U.S. fast-food chains, who have seen traffic from lower-income consumers fall as they raised prices to combat rising labor, food and packaging costs. Wendy’s said Wednesday it is moving “with urgency” to rebuild its menu with a focus on quality and improve marketing and store operations. Wendy’s hired Bob Wright, who formerly led Potbelly, as its president and CEO in May. He’s the fourth CEO to lead the company since 2024. Wendy’s has been closing outdated U.S. restaurants so it can focus on its more profitable locations. The company closed 240 restaurants in 2024 and said earlier this year that it planned to shutter up to 358 locations in 2026. Then, last month, one of the largest U.S. franchisees for Wendy’s filed for bankruptcy protection after the chain tried to terminate its franchise agreement. Michigan-based Meritage Hospitality Group operates 314 Wendy’s restaurants in 15 states. In a letter to the company’s board of directors, Peltz said going private “will deliver the best outcome for the broader stakeholder base.” “Wendy’s sits at a critical juncture,” Peltz wrote. “The external environment has become increasingly challenging given the significant pressures on the U.S. consumer, economic uncertainty, persistent commodity inflation and intensifying competition, particularly within the QSR (quick service restaurant) burger category.” Peltz has invested in companies from Procter & Gamble and Disney to DuPont. According to a regulatory document filed Wednesday, Trian’s stake in Wendy’s totals 16.3%. Peltz considered a take-private bid for Wendy’s in 2022 but told the company in January 2023 that he had decided against it, citing its improved business momentum, according to TD Cowen analyst Andrew Charles. Charles said an independent special committee is expected to evaluate the proposal and both parties have entered into a confidentiality arrangement. “In our view, a take-private makes sense as Wendy’s turnaround is likely to be prolonged given the challenged state of the lower-income consumer and soft state of the quick service burger category,” Charles wrote Wednesday in a note to investors. Wendy’s is scheduled to report its quarterly financial results next week. Analysts expect the company to post earnings of 9 cents per share on sales of $531 million, according to FactSet. Shares rose 93 cents to $7.07 Wednesday. They have fallen 26% since the start of this year.

data.title: Fed expected to hold interest rates steady as inflation tops midterm voters’ concerns
data.description: The Federal Reserve is meeting in Washington this week, where it will consider whether to raise interest rates in an effort to tamp down on inflation. The meetings come at a moment when rising prices are shaping large parts of the U.S. economy and inflation is set to play a key role in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Yet members of the bank’s interest-rate setting committee are widely expected to keep benchmark rates steady this month. There are several reasons why the Fed is unlikely to move on rates Wednesday. But most of them come down to a sense among top officials that the central bank shouldn’t rush into interest rate decisions — and that it definitely shouldn’t do so less than a week out from Election Day. “Inflation remains above our goal,” Michelle Bowman, the Fed’s vice chair for supervision, said Oct. 14. “We have some time to wait and see how financial conditions evolve before we take more action.” The Fed last raised rates by a quarter of a percentage point in September, after a string of monthly inflation readings well above its target of 2% and no signs that prices were coming down anytime soon. “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said at the time. Inflation figures for the month of September, released earlier this month, underscored Warsh’s point, with the annual inflation rate rising to 3.7% from 3.4% the previous month. Some analysts believe Warsh and the Fed will be taking a risk if they vote to hold rates steady, given the trajectory of inflation. “The case for skipping [a rate hike in] October is not terribly compelling,” wrote analysts at Deutsche Bank. Fed officials, however, point to a core tenet of the dual mandate that Congress has assigned to the Fed, of promoting maximum employment while maintaining stable prices. Specifically, the “stable” part, which underpins the Fed’s famously slow and deliberative approach. “I don’t feel urgent that ​we have to decide with a limited set of information,” San Francisco Fed president Mary Daly said in a recent interview. “I think we have the ⁠time that we need.” Another guiding principle at the Fed that is likely tipping expectations about Wednesday is the bank’s tradition of staying far away from politics. If the Fed were to raise rates just days before the midterms, it could, at best, risk looking like a politically motivated decision. At worst, it could influence people’s votes. “We could imagine that all else equal the Fed might prefer to stay out of the headlines for raising rates just ahead of a midterm election where affordability is the principal concern,” wrote the Deutsche Bank analysts. Voters have repeatedly told pollsters that rising prices, especially in the housing and energy sectors, are their primary concerns as they cast their ballots. With control of both the House and the Senate on the line in Tuesday’s election, voters are clear about who they blame for these higher prices: President Donald Trump’s war in Iran and his global tariff regime. The most recent NBC News poll finds Trump’s approval rating at 27% for his handling of the cost of living, and just 29% on his handling the war with Iran. Two-thirds of Americans said the soaring gas prices triggered by Trump’s Iran war were either a “very serious” or “somewhat serious” problem. Likewise, more than half of respondents said that current economic conditions had caused them to change what kinds of groceries they buy. All this adds up to a very difficult political environment for Trump’s fellow Republicans, who are struggling to balance their general support for the president with how unpopular his policies have become with voters. Even the Trump administration, which normally maintains an upbeat view about the economy and inflation, sounded concerned after the most recent inflation reading earlier in the month. “This was a disappointing number,” said Kevin Hassett, director of the White House National Economic Council. Asked by Fox Business hosts why voters had such a negative view of the current economy despite higher spending, Hassett was unsure.“It’s a puzzle that we’re noodling about every day,” he said.

data.title: Want cheap, high-quality meat? Hunt your own game
data.description: Reeling from the sticker shock of supermarket meat prices — and increasingly concerned about their food’s origins — some consumers are taking the problem of finding cheap, high-quality meat into their own hands: by hunting it themselves.

data.title: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start amid high chocolate prices and affordability concerns
data.description: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start this year as U.S. consumers grapple with high living costs and eye-popping chocolate prices. Halloween candy sales fell 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared to the same period last year, according to NielsenIQ, a market research firm. Nielsen also noted an 11.7% decline in candy sales in mid-September, erasing the preseason gains that Halloween candy enjoyed the previous two years. Chris Costagli, a vice president and food thought leader at NielsenIQ, said high gas prices have worsened Americans’ concerns about affordability, and that’s dampening demand for Halloween treats. As of Friday, the average price of a gallon of regular gasoline in the U.S. was $4.29, up nearly 40% from the prior year. “I think what you’re seeing now is a consumer that’s spending so much additional money on fuel and housing and clothing and food,” Costagli said. “Some of the decisions they’re making about Halloween candy, it’s not necessarily because, ‘I notice it’s more expensive than last year,’ it’s, ‘I can’t afford it this year because I’ve paid so much more for so many other things. I just don’t have the financial means to buy it this year.’” Small bags of candy were the only sizes seeing sales growth through mid-October, Costagli noted. Large and extra-large bags were seeing the biggest declines. U.S. candy prices have been climbing faster than the rate of inflation for several years. As of September, candy and gum prices were up 44% over a five-year period, according to government data. Prices for all food eaten at home rose 22.5% in the same period. This week, discount grocer Aldi was advertising a 135-piece variety pack of Mars Inc. chocolate bars — including Milky Way, Trix and Snickers — for $19.87. That’s almost the same price consumers paid for a 250-piece variety pack five years ago. Cocoa prices are the main culprit. Global cocoa prices reached a record high of $10,710 per metric ton in January 2025 because of poor weather in West Africa — which supplies 70% of the world’s chocolate -- and speculative trading in the cocoa futures market, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Cocoa prices had been falling steadily since then, and hit $3,241 per metric ton in March. But they began climbing again in the spring as the Iran war disrupted Africa’s fertilizer supplies. The El Niño weather pattern is also expected to hurt production, with hot, dry conditions expected through February. But Costagli noted that even in cases where prices are lower than last year, consumer demand is muted. The average price of non-chocolate Halloween candies, like gummies and lollipops, was $6.08 per pound in the nine weeks ending Oct. 17, which was about 3% lower than last year, according to Nielsen data. But that didn’t lead to a bump in sales. Sally Lyons Wyatt, a global executive vice president and food industry adviser for the market research company Circana, said one way U.S. consumers have been handling higher grocery prices is by making smaller and more frequent trips to the supermarket and buying products right before they intend to use them. That makes her wonder if shoppers are waiting until closer to Halloween to buy candy this year. “People are very intentional and thoughtful about what they want to consume, not just for holidays, but in general,” she said. “I do believe we will still see softness overall with candy, but I don’t think Halloween is doomed.” The National Confectioners Association, a trade group that represents candy makers like Mars, Smarties Candy Co. and Ferrara Candy Co., said it remains optimistic about Halloween sales. “We are just now entering the peak period for Halloween and consumer enthusiasm remains incredibly strong,” the group said Friday in a statement.

data.title: U.S. airlines favor higher fares over fuller planes as fuel costs squeeze profits
data.description: U.S. airlines are increasingly willing to fly with empty seats rather than slash fares simply to fill ​them, betting that disciplined pricing and flight schedules will help protect profits at a time of soaring fuel costs. The strategy has delivered substantial revenue gains as demand has ‌held up despite sharp fare increases. Yet profits have still been squeezed as jet fuel prices surged roughly 90% since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in February, forcing several major carriers to cut earnings forecasts. Executives at Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Alaska Air Group have emphasized protecting margins over boosting passenger volumes. Their resolve faces a test in 2027. Industry schedules point to more flying capacity, potentially intensifying competition for passengers even as fuel ​prices are expected to stay high and making this year’s substantial fare gains harder to repeat. “If fuel stays elevated, we have to continue to push yield up so that ​we can make a bit of money,” American Chief Financial Officer Devon May told Reuters on Thursday. Yield is the revenue airlines collect for each ⁠mile passengers fly. Six major U.S. airlines plan to grow domestic capacity 3.0% in the fourth quarter from a year earlier and 3.8% in the first quarter of 2027, a sharp acceleration from just ​0.2% growth in the third quarter, according to Airlines for America, citing Cirium data. U.S. air fares rose an average of nearly 23% year-on-year in the seven months through September, far outpacing the 3.6% average ​increase in overall consumer prices, according to Labor Department data. Airlines are still seeking increases. JetBlue Airways initiated a $10 one-way increase in domestic published fares on Wednesday, JP Morgan said, following a similar United-led increase the previous week that Southwest subsequently matched. United said it had nothing further to add, while Southwest said it does not publicly discuss pricing. JetBlue did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A different approach Airlines have long balanced fares against how full their ​planes are. But elevated fuel costs have made executives more willing to sacrifice occupancy and avoid discounts. United’s commercial chief Andrew Nocella offered an example during Wednesday’s earnings call. Its leisure load factor, ​a measure of how many available seats are occupied, fell 1.3 percentage points in the third quarter. Nocella acknowledged that the decline showed “a small amount of elasticity given higher ticket prices,” but called it “a trade we would make ‌every day.” American ⁠Airlines planes flew less full in the third quarter even as passenger yields jumped more than 18%. Finance chief May told Reuters the trade was deliberate. Delta has also been “managing the business for margins,” CEO Ed Bastian said. Across Delta, United, American, Southwest and Alaska, passenger revenue rose nearly $8.8 billion, or 18%, in the third quarter from a year earlier, while passenger traffic increased less than 1%. The divergence shows how much revenue growth now depends on earning more from each passenger rather than carrying more of them. Premium products and changes in passenger mix have also contributed to the gains. The Transportation Security Administration ​screened 2.9% fewer people at U.S. airports in ​the quarter than a year earlier, raising questions ⁠about whether higher fares are beginning to discourage travel. Limited capacity growth and the shutdown of budget carrier Spirit Airlines have also weighed on traffic. Airline executives insisted that demand remains resilient. “Those higher fares are not causing an erosion of volumes,” Southwest CEO Bob Jordan told analysts, after the airline ​reported a nearly 22% increase in average passenger fares in the first nine months of this year. The 2027 test But record revenues have not been ​enough to shield profits from ⁠soaring fuel costs. Gulf Coast spot jet fuel prices have risen from $2.43 a gallon before the war began in February to $4.63 on October 20, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data. Delta and Southwest have cut their annual earnings forecasts, while American expects a full-year loss despite sharply higher passenger revenue. Airlines are now scrutinizing expansion plans. American intends to slow growth considerably next year, with May saying the carrier was reassessing whether additional flights ⁠would generate enough ​revenue to cover their operating costs. Southwest has pledged not to pursue growth at the expense of profitability, while United ​executives have cautioned that airlines’ published 2027 capacity plans may not materialize. Such restraint could help maintain higher fares. But flying less can raise operating costs per seat, while pushing prices higher risks discouraging travelers who have already absorbed steep increases. But airline ​executives say a disciplined approach on capacity can allow the industry to hold on to pricing gains. “We think these yield gains are very sustainable,” May said.

data.title: Etsy to restrict AI-generated content in effort to combat seller slop
data.description: Etsy announced new restrictions Thursday on AI-generated content on its platform, saying it threatens the integrity of its sellers’ work and leaves buyers exposed to fraud. Among the new stipulations: Patterns, recipes, or any other item that involves a buyer “putting in effort to achieve a finished product” cannot be created using AI.Sellers must include at least one unaltered photo of the actual item against a real background.Bot-generated listings are banned. AI-generated art can still be sold on the platform as long as merchants “Play a clear role in what they create and are transparent about the process,” Etsy said in a note to sellers. “Our marketplace only works when buyers and sellers trust each other,” Etsy Vice President of Customer Operations James Ossman wrote in a blog post. “Sellers need clear guidance and confidence that their creativity and craftsmanship will be represented fairly; buyers need to understand what they’re buying and the human involvement behind it. We know we have work to do to uphold this standard on Etsy.” Etsy hosts more than 5 million entrepreneurs, most of whom are women who run one-person businesses out of their homes, according to an annual company report. That distinguishes it from other major e-commerce platforms like Amazon and eBay, though it commands a fraction of those platforms’ revenues. As of 2024, Etsy hosted $10.9 billion-worth of goods’ sales, compared with about $75 billion for eBay and more than $700 billion for Amazon. Some buyers responded positively to Etsy’s announcement. “I can’t explain how infuriating it has been to purchase a crochet pattern, only to open the PDF and realize it’s fully AI-generated, doesn’t make sense, and definitely doesn’t match what the finished product should be,” creator Kara Lynne said on X. The dawn of advanced AI has led to an explosion in AI-generated sales content — and a growing backlash from consumers against what they see as AI slop. A recent social media trend among cafes and restaurants saw owners pledging not to use AI after egregious examples of AI-generated food images in the wild were shared on social media. Major platforms are responding to the growing discontent. Many, including Facebook and Instagram, now work to append labels to images or videos created via AI. Others, like LinkedIn, have added buttons allowing users to report AI-generated content. Snap has banned wholly AI-generated content from its recommendation algorithm, while Spotify recently announced it had removed 50 million AI-generated tracks from its platform. Ossman said Etsy would add a function similar to LinkedIn’s that makes it easier for users to report listings that include misleading AI imagery. He also said Etsy would be using technology to identify misleading imagery and fraudulent listings, with the goal of expanding removals of illicit listings in the coming months. “We’re actively working to address the questions AI raises for our marketplace,” Ossman said in the post. “This work is hard, and we don’t have every answer today. But I believe this is an important moment for Etsy, and that these initial steps are putting us on the right path.”

data.title: Trump promised $2 gas and cheaper groceries. Here’s what voters got instead.
data.description: When voters headed to the polls nearly two years ago, Donald Trump promised them cheaper groceries, gas below $2 a gallon and a wave of new manufacturing jobs. They elected him president — and got the opposite.
